finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: If the attacker can control the wordlist_path and it points to a crafted file or directory name that includes shell metacharacters or control operators, it could lead to command injection.
finding.assumptions: The function `fopen` is used to open the file, and the path provided by the user is directly used without any validation or sanitization.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the untrusted source (argv[3]) is only passed to fopen(). No system, exec, popen, or backtick usage is present in the code. The path is not used in a shell command, so there is no possibility of OS command injection. The code simply opens the file and reads from it; opening a file cannot execute arbitrary commands.

parsed.refutation_attempt: 1) Reviewed the fopen usage at lines 36‑40; the path is passed directly to the system library, which does not execute shell commands, so no command injection is possible. 2) No buffer over-read can occur in this fragment: the buffer sizes used in fgets (256 bytes) and subsequent string handling are all bounded and safe. 3) The reported source (argv[3]) is a normal file path input; the code correctly checks the file opening result and does not use the path in a shell context. 4) No other code paths or dead code create a vulnerability. The claim that fopen could cause a buffer over-read or command injection is unsupported by the source code.
